2026-08-04 — the register held again: the three availability rows and the Spotify quota policy were re-fetched today and every value came back identical, and the four npm package-metadata rows and four spec-behaviour rows were deliberately NOT re-fetched and keep their earlier dates rather than being silently bumped. No page copy needed correcting and NO PAGE WAS WRITTEN.

Why no page. All six measured buyer queries have had a page since 2026-08-02, and today's competitor-gap list is character-for-character the same seven domains as yesterday's. Six of them are not products this host could honestly compare itself to, for reasons recorded under github-repo-public; the seventh, htmlelements.com, was re-fetched today rather than dismissed on yesterday's word, and its own documentation confirms it ships no receipt component and no image export. The stronger reason to rest is measurement, not the gap list: this host has 0 impressions, 0 indexed URLs and four content pages published in six days, none of which has been indexed yet. There is no evidence on this host about what works, because nothing has been measured. A fifth page written before the first measurement is a guess, and four unindexed pages do not become more findable by adding a fifth.

What the 2026-08-03 sitemap fix actually did — read the list, do not infer it. GET /webmasters/v3/sites/sc-domain:kynth.studio/sitemaps today returns 129 sitemaps and tearline.kynth.studio/sitemap.xml IS among them: lastSubmitted 2026-08-03T14:05:11Z, lastDownloaded 2026-08-03T14:05:13Z (two seconds later), isPending false, warnings 0, errors 0, 5 URLs submitted, 0 indexed. The effect is already visible in today's URL inspections: /docs, /receipt-ui and /spotify-receipt-generator have moved from "URL is unknown to Google" to "Discovered - currently not indexed" within 24 hours, while the root and /dom-to-png are still unknown. So the remaining pages-unknown-to-google finding is now a WAITING STATE, not an unfixed defect, and a future run should not re-diagnose it. Both discovery paths were confirmed intact: IndexNow submitted all 5 URLs on 2026-08-03T15:56Z under the estate key b00c520655b742c4b66519deb4181076 (which this repo serves from public/), and kynth.studio's own landing links tearline.kynth.studio, so Google has a crawl path from an established host as well as from the feed.

One finding examined and deliberately left alone: the audit's low-severity multiple-h1. The landing's second <h1> is src/components/sections/HeroSection.tsx:233 — the word "Meridian" inside the live <tear-line> demo. It is sample receipt content, and the code panel beside it prints that exact markup under the label "renders to". Swapping it to an h2 would visibly shrink and letter-space the demo (tearline.js:99-100 style ::slotted(h1) and ::slotted(h2) differently), and changing only the rendered half would make the panel lie about what the component does. Google does not penalise multiple h1s. The demo stays as written; do not "fix" this on a later run.

2026-08-03 — the register held completely: all four rows re-fetched today (three availability, plus the Spotify quota policy) came back identical, and the four npm package-metadata rows and four spec-behaviour rows were deliberately NOT re-fetched and keep their earlier dates rather than being silently bumped. No page copy needed correcting and no page was written, because all six measured buyer queries already have a page as of 2026-08-02 and today's competitor-gap list (developer.mozilla.org, community.weweb.io, addtoany.com, ryanfeigenbaum.com, htmlelements.com, plus the recurring github.com and stackoverflow.com) contains no product this host could honestly compare itself to — MDN, Stack Overflow, GitHub, the WeWeb forum and a personal blog are third-party surfaces, and AddToAny (share buttons, not share images) and htmlelements.com (an enterprise component suite with no receipt component and no image export) do a different job, so a comparison page against either would be a category error with a table around it. The day's real finding was not in this file: tearline.kynth.studio/sitemap.xml had NEVER been submitted to Google Search Console. 126 estate sitemaps were registered on sc-domain:kynth.studio and this host was absent, because the bulk submitter discovers hosts from kynth-os/apps/* and Tearline lives in its own standalone repo. Four prior runs recorded pages-unknown-to-google as 'nothing to do by hand'; that was wrong, and the check that would have caught it is reading the submitted-sitemap list rather than reasoning about the crawl files. It was submitted today (HTTP 204, registered pending). Nothing about this belongs in the claims array — it is not a claim made to a buyer — but it is written here because this is the file a future run reads first.

Dated-claim register. Tearline is a developer library, not a regulated product, so for its first four pages it made almost no claims about the world that decay on a calendar — what it claimed was that external artefacts exist and are reachable, that four npm packages have certain metadata, and that a handful of browser behaviours work a certain way. 2026-08-02 changed that. The fifth page, /spotify-receipt-generator, is the first surface on this host that publishes somebody else's POLICY, and policy decays far faster than spec behaviour: the two new entries (spotify-quota-modes, spotify-top-items-endpoint) are now the highest-churn rows in this file and the quota one is page-breaking if it moves, because the page's whole argument follows from the individual-versus-organisation split. It was fetched twice on the same day, from the same source, precisely because of that. On 2026-08-02 the three availability entries were re-fetched and all held: tearline.js still 200s at 12,756 bytes, the npm package is still unpublished, the GitHub repository is still private. Nothing drifted and no existing page copy needed correcting. The four npm package-metadata rows and the four spec-behaviour rows were NOT re-fetched today and keep their earlier dates rather than being silently bumped. One thing this register deliberately does not contain: any claim about the receipt-generator sites currently serving this query. A search for them returns a field of near-identical domains whose operators are not identifiable from their own pages, and no ranked list of them was published, because a list assembled from search results is a guess with a table around it. The page says so out loud in its sources section.

claims.note: Fetched from MDN on 2026-07-31; the wording on the page is a paraphrase of the 'Security and tainted canvases' section, not a quote. claims.claim: The naming and lifecycle rules a custom element must satisfy
claims.value: the name must start with a lowercase letter and contain a hyphen; observedAttributes is a static array of attribute names, and attributeChangedCallback() fires after an observed attribute is initialised when the declaration is first parsed
claims.note: Fetched from MDN on 2026-08-01. The hyphen rule is quoted on the page; the first-parse timing of attributeChangedCallback() is paraphrased. claims.claim: Which declaration wins between a shadow tree and the outer document
claims.value: in cascade sorting order, when declarations come from different encapsulation contexts the outer context wins for normal rules and the inner context wins for important rules
claims.sourceTitle: W3C — CSS Cascade and Inheritance Level 5
claims.note: Fetched from the W3C TR on 2026-08-01. This is the normative source for a claim the codebase and llms.txt had been making in their own words since launch — that ::slotted() rules 'lose to your own CSS'. MDN's ::slotted and Using-shadow-DOM pages were both checked first and neither states the cascade direction, so the spec is the citation. The claim is now sourced everywhere it appears rather than asserted.

claims.claim: How many users a Spotify Web API app may serve, and who may apply to lift the cap
claims.value: development mode is capped at 5 authenticated users and requires the owner to hold Spotify Premium; extended quota mode lifts the cap but since 15 May 2025 is open to organisations only, with stated criteria including a registered business entity and at least 250k MAUs
claims.note: Fetched TWICE from developer.spotify.com on 2026-08-02 — once for the mode definitions and once specifically to confirm the eligibility bullets and the policy date, because the entire page turns on this claim and a single summarising read was not enough to publish on. Both reads agreed. Quoted verbatim on the page: "Up to 5 authenticated Spotify users can use an app that is in development mode", "Spotify only accepts applications from organizations (not individuals)", "Maintaining a minimum of active users (at least 250k MAUs)" and "Established Business Entity (legally registered business or organisation)". This is the fastest-decaying claim the host publishes: it is vendor POLICY, not spec behaviour, and it already changed once (May 2025). Treat a change here as page-breaking, not cosmetic — the page's whole argument, and its Plan B section, follow from the individual/organisation split. Re-fetched 2026-08-03, one day after publication, because this is the fastest-decaying row in the file and the page's whole argument follows from it. All four quoted strings returned identical: "Up to 5 authenticated Spotify users can use an app that is in development mode", "as of May 15th 2025, Spotify only accepts applications from organizations (not individuals)", "Maintaining a minimum of active users (at least 250k MAUs)" and "Established Business Entity (legally registered business or organisation)". The Premium requirement also re-confirmed verbatim: "The app owner must have a Spotify Premium account for apps in development mode to function." No drift; /spotify-receipt-generator needs no correction. Re-fetched 2026-08-04, the third read of this row in three days, because it remains the fastest-decaying claim on the host. All five quoted strings returned identical again: "Up to 5 authenticated Spotify users can use an app that is in development mode", "The app owner must have a Spotify Premium account for apps in development mode to function.", "as of May 15th 2025, Spotify only accepts applications from organizations (not individuals)", "Maintaining a minimum of active users (at least 250k MAUs)" and "Established Business Entity (legally registered business or organisation)". claims.claim: The endpoint, scope and parameter limits behind every listening-history receipt
claims.value: GET /me/top/{type} (artists|tracks), scope user-top-read; time_range is long_term (~1 year of data) | medium_term (~last 6 months) | short_term (~last 4 weeks), default medium_term; limit default 20, minimum 1, maximum 50; offset default 0
claims.sourceTitle: Spotify Web API reference — Get User's Top Items
claims.note: Fetched from the Spotify Web API reference on 2026-08-02. The time_range descriptions are quoted verbatim on the page. Load-bearing for the page's central observation — that the "last month / 6 months / all time" and "top 10 / top 50" controls shared by every receipt generator are the API's parameter list showing through the UI, not a design convention. It is also the source for the page telling readers NOT to label long_term "all time": Spotify describes it as calculated from about a year of data. If Spotify renames a time_range value or moves the limit ceiling, that sentence and the comparison it supports both need rewriting.
